prompt: Which of these is a tester's security work rather than a penetration tester's?
hint: It runs every day, not once a year.

choices.text: Chaining three small weaknesses into one way in, over two weeks of trying
choices.why: That is what a penetration test is good at: combinations, by a specialist, inside a scope.

choices.text: A test that a second customer's token is refused the first one's booking
choices.why: Right. A requirement turned into a regression test that runs on every change.

choices.text: Signing the document that authorises an attack on production
choices.why: Only the system's owner can authorise a test; a tester does not sign their own permission.

choices.text: Proving the defences fail by getting into the live site
choices.why: Getting in is the penetration tester's job, under written permission, and not a test plan's.

prompt: Which of these is an abuse case for the booking feature?
hint: Somebody wants what they should not have.

choices.text: As a customer, I book seat 12 for tonight and get a booking number back
choices.why: That is the use case itself: what a customer does to get what they are entitled to.

choices.text: As a customer, I ask for somebody else's booking and am refused
choices.why: Right. The story told by somebody after what is not theirs, with a refusal as the expected result.

choices.text: As staff, I list every booking for tonight's show
choices.why: Staff are allowed the list; this is a use case for a different role.

choices.text: As a customer, I book a seat that is taken and get a 409
choices.why: A functional rule about seats. Nobody is asking for something that belongs to somebody else.

prompt: Match each part of a penetration test to what it says.
hint: The table in the first reading section.

pairs.right: a signed document from the system's owner
which addresses and accounts are in, and which are out
when, how, what is never done, and who to call
each finding, how it was reached and how to fix it

right_distractors: the list of tests that passed

prompt: A colleague wants to type a single quote into the card form of the theatre's payment provider, from the staging server, to see whether it errors. What do you tell them?
hint: Whose system is the card form?

choices.text: Go ahead: a single quote is a harmless probe
choices.why: Harmless or not, it is a probe of a system you were not invited to test.

choices.text: Go ahead, since the request leaves from our own staging server
choices.why: Where the request starts does not matter; the provider's system is the one being probed.

choices.text: Not without the provider's written permission
choices.why: Right. Their system is outside your scope, and their own policy decides what may be tested.

choices.text: Only at night, when nobody is paying for tickets
choices.why: The hour changes who is inconvenienced, not whose system it is or who agreed.

prompt: Match each kind of scanner to what it reads.
hint: Most of the acronyms name a place.

pairs.right: the source code, without running it
every file and every past commit
the running service, over HTTP, from outside
an agent inside the running process

right_distractors: the people who use the service

prompt: Why does SCA have to run on a schedule as well as on every change?
hint: What changes while your code stays the same?

choices.text: Advisories are published while your code stays the same
choices.why: Right. Yesterday's clean commit is vulnerable today, and only a scheduled run notices.

choices.text: It is too slow to run on every pull request
choices.why: pip-audit took seconds in this course; speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Dependencies upgrade themselves overnight
choices.why: A pinned version stays where it was pinned; the advisory database is what moves.

choices.text: Its report expires after a day and has to be renewed
choices.why: A report does not expire; the world it was checked against changes.

prompt: Somebody deletes the owner check from account.py. Which kind of scanner reports it?
hint: Which tool knows that a booking belongs to somebody?

choices.text: SAST, which knows the shape of a missing check
choices.why: A missing line has no shape to match: what is left is valid, ordinary code.

choices.text: DAST, because the route starts answering 200
choices.why: A 200 to a signed-in customer is what the route is meant to do; DAST cannot tell whose booking it was.

choices.text: None of them; a test with two customers does
choices.why: Right. The rule lives in the business, and the test is what holds it.

choices.text: SCA, because the file changed since the last scan
choices.why: SCA reads the dependency list, which did not change at all.

prompt: Which kind of tool sends HTTP requests to the running service and sees only the answers?

choices.text: SAST
choices.why: SAST reads the source code without running it.

choices.text: IAST
choices.why: IAST is inside the process, so it sees more than answers.

choices.text: DAST
choices.why: Right. Dynamic analysis, from outside, like a browser would.

choices.text: SCA
choices.why: SCA reads the dependency list.

prompt: Where does account.py find the path of its database?
hint: The first lines of the file.

choices.text: In a settings file beside it
choices.why: There is no settings file; nothing about the deployment is written down in one.

choices.text: In ACCOUNT_DB, with data/account.db when it is unset
choices.why: Right. The environment decides, and the default works on your machine.

choices.text: In a constant fixed in the code at data/account.db
choices.why: That is only the default; the environment variable takes precedence.

choices.text: On the command line, as its first argument
choices.why: account.py reads no arguments at all.

prompt: After how many failed sign-ins within five minutes does account.py refuse a name, even with the right password?
Why is somebody else's booking answered with 404 rather than 403?
hint: What would a 403 tell a stranger?

choices.text: A 403 would end the session of whoever asked
choices.why: No status ends a session; logout and expiry do.

choices.text: So the answer does not reveal that the booking exists
choices.why: Right. Somebody else's booking and no booking look the same from outside.

choices.text: The route does not know who sent the request
choices.why: It does: `who` found the session before the owner check runs.

choices.text: HTTP does not allow a 403 in answer to a GET
choices.why: A 403 is a valid answer to any method; the staff route uses it.

prompt: Why does the two-customer test first check that the owner gets a 200?
hint: What else would make the second request answer 404?

choices.text: To make the booking exist before the second customer asks
choices.why: `book` already made it; the 200 proves something different.

choices.text: So a 404 means refused, not broken
choices.why: Right. A route that fails for everyone also answers 404, and the control rules that out.

choices.text: Because unittest wants a passing assertion first
choices.why: unittest has no such rule; assertions may come in any order.

choices.text: To wait until the server thread has started
choices.why: setUpModule started it before any test ran.

prompt: Running a suite against copies of the code, each altered in one place, to see which test notices, is called ___ testing.
You comment out the line ending in # CSRF check and the whole suite stays green. What have you learnt?
hint: What is a test that cannot fail worth?

choices.text: No test holds that defence, whatever its name says
choices.why: Right. One defence removed should turn one test red; here nothing turned.

choices.text: The check was never needed, so it can go
choices.why: A green suite says nothing was tested, not that nothing was needed.

choices.text: SameSite=Lax already covers it, so green is the right answer
choices.why: SameSite is a second layer and old browsers ignore it; the test should still see the token check go.

choices.text: The mutation tool missed the line
choices.why: There was no tool: you made the copy, and the suite ran against it.

prompt: Put in order the steps that prove a defence's test is worth having.
hint: Green first, then take something away.
items: run the suite against the real service and see it green
copy the service with the one guarding line commented out
run the same suite against the copy
see the test written for that line fail, and only that one

prompt: A team runs SAST, SCA and secret scanning on every pull request, a DAST scan of staging every week and a penetration test every year. Which risk is still unwatched between penetration tests?
hint: Which of these is particular to this application?

choices.text: A library version with a published advisory
choices.why: SCA on every pull request looks for exactly that.

choices.text: A customer reading another's booking
choices.why: Right. A business rule no scanner knows; only a test with two customers watches it.

choices.text: An API key committed to the repository
choices.why: Secret scanning on every pull request is there for that.

choices.text: A security header missing from the staging pages
choices.why: The weekly DAST scan of staging reports missing headers.

prompt: Which of these may you send? Choose every one that is allowed.

choices.text: A second customer's token asking account.py on your VM for the first one's booking
choices.why: Right. Your own service, on 127.0.0.1.

choices.text: A single quote in the search box of the page your VM serves
choices.why: Right. A benign probe of your own page.

choices.text: The same probes against the theatre's live site, which runs the same code
choices.why: Same code, somebody else's system: it needs the owner's written permission.

choices.text: A text file sent as an avatar to account.py on your VM
choices.why: Right. The upload probe, against your own service.
